content: The placement of central venous catheters (CVCs) in individuals with cancer is associated with an increased risk of thrombosis. Thrombosis can lead to the removal of the CVC, which may delay treatment and contribute to morbidity and mortality related to thrombosis. This study aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of anticoagulation therapy for preventing thrombosis in cancer patients with CVCs. A systematic review was conducted, including randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed the benefits and risks of various anticoagulants, such as unfractionated heparin (UFH), low-molecular-weight heparin (LMWH), vitamin K antagonists (VKA), and fondaparinux, or compared these agents against each other. The outcomes analyzed included all-cause mortality, symptomatic catheter-related venous thromboembolism (VTE), pulmonary embolism (PE), major and minor bleeding, catheter-related infections, thrombocytopenia, and health-related quality of life (HRQoL). The certainty of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Thirteen RCTs involving 3420 participants were included in the analysis. Seven trials compared LMWH to no LMWH, six trials compared VKA to no VKA, and three trials compared LMWH to VKA. 1. LMWH versus No LMWH: Six RCTs (1537 participants) compared LMWH to no LMWH in adults. LMWH likely reduced the incidence of symptomatic catheter-related VTE within three months of follow-up (risk ratio [RR] 0.43, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.22 to 0.81; moderate-certainty evidence). This corresponds to 38 fewer cases of VTE per 1000 individuals. The effect of LMWH on mortality at three months was uncertain (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.53 to 1.26; low-certainty evidence). The evidence was also inconclusive regarding the impact of LMWH on major bleeding (RR 1.49, 95% CI 0.06 to 36.28; very low-certainty evidence), minor bleeding (RR 1.35, 95% CI 0.62 to 2.92; low-certainty evidence), and thrombocytopenia (RR 1.03, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.33; low-certainty evidence). 2. VKA versus No VKA: Five RCTs (1599 participants) compared low-dose VKA to no VKA in adults. The evidence did not confirm or exclude a beneficial or harmful effect of VKA on mortality (RR 0.99, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.55; low-certainty evidence) or symptomatic catheter-related VTE (RR 0.61, 95% CI 0.23 to 1.64; low-certainty evidence). The impact of VKA on major bleeding (RR 7.14, 95% CI 0.88 to 57.78; low-certainty evidence), minor bleeding (RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.26; low-certainty evidence), premature catheter removal (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.30 to 2.24; low-certainty evidence), and catheter-related infections (RR 1.17, 95% CI 0.74 to 1.85; low-certainty evidence) was also inconclusive. 3. LMWH versus VKA: Three RCTs (641 participants) compared LMWH to VKA in adults. The evidence did not confirm or exclude a beneficial or harmful effect of LMWH compared to VKA on mortality (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.56 to 1.59; low-certainty evidence), symptomatic catheter-related VTE (RR 1.83, 95% CI 0.44 to 7.61; very low-certainty evidence), or pulmonary embolism (RR 1.70, 95% CI 0.74 to 3.92; low-certainty evidence). The effect of LMWH on major bleeding (RR 3.11, 95% CI 0.13 to 73.11; very low-certainty evidence) and minor bleeding (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.20 to 4.61; very low-certainty evidence) was also uncertain. However, LMWH likely increased the risk of thrombocytopenia compared to VKA (RR 1.69, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.39; moderate-certainty evidence), with an estimated 149 more cases of thrombocytopenia per 1000 individuals. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that LMWH likely reduces the risk of catheter-related VTE compared to no LMWH, but its effects on mortality and bleeding remain uncertain. The effects of VKA on mortality and catheter-related VTE are also inconclusive. When comparing LMWH to VKA, the evidence does not clearly favor one over the other for most outcomes, except for a likely increased risk of thrombocytopenia with LMWH. Patients with cancer and CVCs should carefully weigh the potential benefits of reduced thromboembolic complications against the risks and burdens associated with anticoagulation therapy.
